content.statement: One machine with a single IP address can run a web server on port 443 and a database on port 5432 at the same time.

remember: The IP address finds the machine and the port finds the program, so one address can serve many programs.

content.prompt: npm run dev fails with "Error: listen EADDRINUSE: address already in use :::3000". What does it mean?

options.text: Another process is already listening on port 3000
A firewall is blocking incoming traffic on port 3000
Port 3000 can only be opened by the root user
Another device on the network already uses this IP address

remember: EADDRINUSE means some process already listens on that port; stop it or start your server on another port.

content.prompt: Match each port with the service that uses it by default.

right.text: HTTPS
PostgreSQL
SSH
DNS

remember: Well-known defaults: 22 SSH, 53 DNS, 80 HTTP, 443 HTTPS, 5432 PostgreSQL; a URL without a port uses its scheme's default.

content.prompt: The api container fails with "connection refused" on port 5432, although the db container is up and healthy. Find the bug.
content.code:
services:
  db:
    image: postgres:17
    environment:
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: dev
  api:
    build: ./api
    environment:
      DB_HOST: localhost
      DB_PORT: "5432"
    depends_on:
      - db

fixes.text: Add a healthcheck so api starts after db is ready
Set DB_HOST to db, the Compose service name
Publish the database port with ports: "5432:5432"

remember: Inside a container, localhost is that container itself; reach another Compose service by its service name.

content.prompt: Fill the blank so a phone on the same Wi-Fi can open the dev server at http://<laptop-ip>:8080.

remember: A server bound to 127.0.0.1 or localhost accepts only connections from the same machine; 0.0.0.0 listens on every network interface.

content.statement: UDP guarantees that packets arrive in the same order they were sent.

remember: UDP packets can be lost, duplicated or reordered; only TCP gives you a reliable, ordered stream.

content.prompt: Which of these is a better fit for UDP than for TCP?

options.text: Live voice in a video call

remember: UDP suits real-time data where a late packet is worthless; anything that must arrive complete uses TCP.

content.prompt: A browser opens a plain HTTP/1.1 connection, sends one request, gets the response and closes the connection. Order the packets.

steps.text: The client sends ACK
The client sends SYN
The client sends the HTTP request
The server replies with SYN-ACK
One side sends FIN to close the connection

remember: TCP opens with SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK before any data flows, and a FIN starts closing the connection.

content.prompt: Three of these usually run over UDP. Which one runs over TCP?

items.text: DNS lookups for a site's address
Audio and video in a WebRTC call
Player positions in a fast online game
An SSH session to a server

remember: SSH needs every byte in order, so it uses TCP; DNS lookups and real-time media and games use UDP.

content.prompt: The client writes one valid JSON object per line, but under load JSON.parse throws SyntaxError on the server. Find the bug.

fixes.text: Call socket.setNoDelay(true) so each write arrives alone
Wrap JSON.parse in try/catch and skip bad chunks
Buffer the chunks and parse only complete lines

remember: TCP is a byte stream without message boundaries: one data event can hold half a message or several, so frame messages yourself.

content.statement: Each time you open a website, your browser asks the root DNS servers for its address.

remember: Browsers ask a nearby recursive resolver, and every step caches answers, so root servers are rarely contacted.

content.prompt: You moved shop.hr to a new server and updated its A record. For the next hour some users still reach the old server. What is the most likely reason?

options.text: The registry publishes A record changes once a day
Browsers keep an IP for as long as the domain is registered
Resolvers serve the cached old record until its TTL expires
The old server keeps answering because it holds the certificate

remember: DNS answers are cached for their TTL; lower the TTL before a planned move so the change takes effect quickly.

content.prompt: Three of these are published in DNS records. Which one is never put in DNS?

items.text: The IPv4 address of shop.hr
The private key of shop.hr's TLS certificate
The mail servers that accept mail for shop.hr
An alias from www.shop.hr to shop.hr

remember: DNS is a public directory of names: addresses (A, AAAA), aliases (CNAME), mail servers (MX) and text (TXT), never secrets.

content.prompt: Nothing is cached anywhere yet. Order the steps that resolve shop.hr.

steps.text: The resolver asks a .hr server, which refers it to shop.hr's name servers
The browser and OS find nothing cached and ask the configured resolver
The resolver caches the answer for its TTL and returns it
The resolver asks a root server, which refers it to the .hr servers
The resolver asks shop.hr's authoritative server and gets the A record

remember: An uncached lookup walks root, then TLD, then the domain's authoritative server, and each answer is cached for its TTL.

content.prompt: These records are published. What does the command print?
content.code:
# www.shop.hr.        CNAME  shop.edge-cdn.net.
# shop.edge-cdn.net.  A      203.0.113.7

$ dig +short www.shop.hr A

options.text: Nothing, because www.shop.hr has no A record

remember: Resolvers follow CNAME aliases for you: asking for the A record of an alias returns the CNAME and the final address.

content.statement: The part of a URL after # is sent to the server with the HTTP request.

remember: The fragment after # stays in the browser; it is used for in-page anchors and client-side routing, never sent to the server.

content.prompt: In https://shop.hr/search?q=shoes&page=2, which part is the path?

remember: The path is the part between the host and the ?; the query string comes after the ?.

content.prompt: What does this print?
content.code:
const u = new URL("https://shop.hr:8443/cart?id=7");
console.log(u.hostname, u.port);

remember: hostname is the name alone, host adds the port, and port holds the number written in the URL.

content.prompt: Searching for "rock & roll" returns results for "rock" only. Find the bug.

fixes.text: Wrap term in encodeURIComponent()
Wrap the whole url in encodeURI()
Replace the spaces in term with +

remember: Encode every value you put into a query string with encodeURIComponent or URLSearchParams; a raw & or = splits it.

content.prompt: Fill the blank so the code prints the URL in the comment.

remember: A relative URL without a leading slash resolves against the base's directory; a leading slash replaces the whole path.

content.statement: Every HTTP response carries a status code, such as 200 or 404, that tells the client what happened.

remember: A response is a status code, headers and an optional body; the code says whether and how the request succeeded.

content.prompt: A client POSTs JSON to an API. Which request header tells the server what format the body is in?

remember: Content-Type describes the body being sent; Accept says which formats the client wants back.

content.prompt: http://shop.hr/login answers 301 with Location: https://shop.hr/login, and that page answers 200. What does the command print?

remember: curl does not follow redirects unless you pass -L; without it you see the 3xx response itself.

content.prompt: Several sites share one IP address. Fill the blank so the server knows which site this request is for.

remember: HTTP/1.1 requires a Host header; it lets one server at one IP address host many sites.

content.prompt: The API's JSON parser leaves the body empty and it answers 400 "items is required", although order.items is set. Find the bug.

fixes.text: Pass body: order without JSON.stringify
Add "Content-Type": "application/json" to headers
Change the method to PUT

remember: A JSON body needs Content-Type: application/json; fetch labels a string body text/plain, and JSON parsers skip it.

content.statement: Cache-Control: no-cache tells the browser not to store the response at all.

remember: no-cache means store it but revalidate before every reuse; no-store is the directive that forbids keeping a copy.

content.prompt: The browser holds a copy with ETag: "v7". It sends If-None-Match: "v7" and the resource has not changed. How should the server answer?

options.text: 200 OK with the full body and the same ETag

remember: A matching If-None-Match gets 304 Not Modified without a body, and the browser reuses its stored copy.

content.prompt: app.4f9c2a.js gets a new file name whenever its content changes. Fill the blank so browsers may reuse it for a year without revalidating, even on a reload.
content.code:
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/javascript
Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, ____

remember: Fingerprinted files can be cached for a year with immutable; a new file name, not revalidation, delivers updates.

content.prompt: The browser receives this response from a CDN at exactly 10:00:00 GMT (clocks in sync). A script requests the same URL at 10:02:00. What does the browser do?
content.code:
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Date: Sat, 24 Oct 2026 09:51:00 GMT
Cache-Control: max-age=600
Age: 540
Content-Type: application/json

options.text: Goes to the network; the copy went stale at 10:01:00
Reuses the stored copy; it stays fresh until 10:10:00
Reuses the stored copy; Age only matters to proxies
Goes to the network; responses with Age are never stored

remember: max-age counts from when the origin produced the response, and Age tells how much of it a CDN has already used up.

content.prompt: Match each Cache-Control directive with what it allows.

right.text: Shared caches treat it as fresh for 60 s, overriding max-age
Store it, but check with the server before every reuse
Reuse it freely while fresh, but never serve it stale without checking
Only the user's browser may store it, not a CDN

remember: no-cache revalidates every time, must-revalidate only once stale; private keeps CDNs out and s-maxage sets their lifetime.

content.statement: JavaScript on the page cannot read a cookie that was set with the HttpOnly flag.

remember: HttpOnly hides a cookie from document.cookie; the browser still sends it with matching requests.

content.prompt: How does a server store a cookie in the browser?

options.text: With a Cookie header in its response
With a Set-Cookie header in its response
With an Authorization header in its response
By putting the cookie in the JSON response body

remember: Servers set cookies with Set-Cookie in a response; browsers send them back in the Cookie request header.

content.prompt: Match each Set-Cookie attribute with its effect.

right.text: Deleted right away
Removed when the browser session ends
Also sent to subdomains such as api.shop.hr
Sent only for URLs under /admin

remember: Domain widens a cookie to subdomains, Path narrows it to a URL prefix, and Max-Age or Expires decide how long it lives.

content.prompt: The browser stored these cookies from https://shop.hr. A page on https://evil.example then submits a form with method POST to https://shop.hr/transfer. Which Cookie header does that request carry?
content.code:
Set-Cookie: a=1; Secure; SameSite=Strict
Set-Cookie: b=2; Secure; SameSite=Lax
Set-Cookie: c=3; Secure; SameSite=None

remember: From another site, SameSite=Lax cookies ride only on top-level GET navigations; a cross-site POST carries only SameSite=None cookies.

content.prompt: After logout the browser keeps sending the sid cookie with requests to /app. Find the bug.

fixes.text: Clear it with res.cookie("sid", "") instead
Delete it in the browser with document.cookie
Pass path: "/app" to clearCookie as well

remember: A cookie is identified by name, domain and path; deleting it needs a Set-Cookie with the same domain and path.

content.statement: http://localhost:5173 and http://localhost:5080 are the same origin.

remember: An origin is scheme, host and port; a different port alone makes it a different origin.

content.prompt: A fetch from https://app.shop.hr to https://api.shop.hr works in curl but fails in the browser with a CORS error. Where does the fix belong?

options.text: In fetch: pass mode: "no-cors" to skip the check
In fetch: send an Access-Control-Allow-Origin request header
On the server of app.shop.hr: add the header to the HTML page
On the API: return Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.shop.hr

remember: CORS is permission from the server you call: only its Access-Control-Allow-Origin response header lets the page read the response.

content.prompt: Three of these URLs are cross-origin for a page on https://shop.hr. Which one is the same origin?

items.text: https://shop.hr:443/api/cart
http://shop.hr/api/cart
https://www.shop.hr/api/cart
https://shop.hr:8443/api/cart

remember: Origins compare scheme, host and port; writing the default port 443 changes nothing, any other difference does.

content.prompt: A page on https://app.shop.hr calls fetch with method PUT and a JSON body to https://api.shop.hr/items/7. Order what happens.

steps.text: The server answers 204 with Access-Control-Allow-Methods including PUT
The browser sends OPTIONS with Access-Control-Request-Method: PUT
The browser checks Access-Control-Allow-Origin on the PUT response
The browser sends the PUT request with its JSON body
The fetch promise resolves with the response

remember: A non-simple request is preceded by an OPTIONS preflight; only if the server allows it does the browser send the real request.

content.prompt: The fetch to /me fails with a CORS error, while the same fetch without credentials: "include" works. Find the bug.

fixes.text: Send https://app.shop.hr instead of *
Remove the Access-Control-Allow-Credentials header
Add Cookie to Access-Control-Allow-Headers

remember: For credentialed requests the server must name the exact origin and send Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true; * is rejected.

content.statement: On an HTTPS site, someone on the same Wi-Fi network can read the query strings of the URLs you request.

remember: TLS encrypts the whole HTTP message, including path, query and headers; the network still sees which server you contact.

content.prompt: What does a server's TLS certificate let the browser check?

options.text: That the site is free of malware and phishing
That the company behind the site is trustworthy
That the server controls the domain name in the URL
That nobody can see which IP address you connect to

remember: A certificate proves the server controls the domain name; it says nothing about whether the site is honest or safe.

content.prompt: Order the steps when a browser opens https://shop.hr on a new connection.

steps.text: The client checks the certificate chain and that it covers shop.hr
The client sends ClientHello with its TLS versions and the name shop.hr
The browser sends the HTTP request, encrypted
The client and server open a TCP connection
The server answers with its chosen settings and its certificate

remember: TCP connects first, then the TLS handshake proves the server's identity and agrees on keys, and only then does HTTP data flow.

content.prompt: A certificate lists only *.shop.hr. Three of these hostnames get a certificate name error. Which one is covered?

items.text: shop.hr
api.shop.hr
api.v2.shop.hr
shop.hr.edge-cdn.net

remember: A wildcard covers exactly one label: *.shop.hr matches api.shop.hr but neither shop.hr nor api.v2.shop.hr.

content.prompt: certbot wrote cert.pem, chain.pem, fullchain.pem and privkey.pem. The site opens in desktop Chrome, but curl fails with "unable to get local issuer certificate". Find the bug.

fixes.text: Point ssl_certificate at chain.pem
Point ssl_certificate at fullchain.pem
Add ssl_protocols TLSv1.3; to the server block

remember: Send the intermediate certificates too (fullchain.pem); some browsers patch a missing chain, but curl and many clients do not.

content.statement: Over an open WebSocket connection, the server can send a message without the client asking for it first.

remember: A WebSocket is a two-way channel: after the handshake either side can send a message at any time.

content.prompt: Which feature fits WebSocket better than plain HTTP requests?

options.text: A live quiz where both players see each answer instantly

remember: Use WebSocket when the server must push updates as they happen; one-off loads are simpler over plain HTTP.

content.prompt: The page is served from https://quiz.shop.hr. Fill the blank so the browser allows the connection.

remember: Pages served over HTTPS must use wss://, WebSocket over TLS; plain ws:// is blocked as mixed content.

content.prompt: The server accepts this WebSocket handshake. Which status line does it answer with?
content.code:
GET /live HTTP/1.1
Host: quiz.shop.hr
Upgrade: websocket
Connection: Upgrade
Sec-WebSocket-Key: dGhlIHNhbXBsZSBub25jZQ==
Sec-WebSocket-Version: 13

remember: A WebSocket starts as an HTTP/1.1 GET with Upgrade: websocket, and 101 Switching Protocols turns that connection into a WebSocket.

content.prompt: Chat WebSockets behind a load balancer drop after exactly 60 seconds without messages, while busy ones stay open. What is the usual fix?

options.text: Move the chat to HTTP/2 so the connection is shared
Add Connection: keep-alive to the handshake request
Send a ping or heartbeat message every 30 seconds
Switch from ws:// to wss:// so the proxy cannot read it

remember: Proxies and load balancers close idle connections; a periodic ping keeps a quiet WebSocket alive and detects dead ones.

content.statement: Behind a reverse proxy, the app sees the proxy's IP address as the source of each connection, not the user's.

remember: The app's TCP peer is the proxy, so the user's address must be passed along in a header such as X-Forwarded-For.

content.prompt: Users open https://shop.hr. nginx on that server forwards requests to a Node app on port 3000. Which program do the users' browsers connect to?

options.text: The Node app on port 3000; nginx only watches
Both nginx and the Node app, in parallel
The DNS server, which relays requests to the app
nginx, which opens its own connection to the app

remember: A reverse proxy is the only server the client talks to; it makes its own connection to the app behind it.

content.prompt: A client at 198.51.100.4 sends a request with the header X-Forwarded-For: 10.1.1.1 to this nginx. What X-Forwarded-For value does the app receive?

remember: Each proxy appends the address it got the request from, so only the entries your own proxies added can be trusted.

content.prompt: Match each nginx directive with its job in a reverse proxy.

right.text: Lists several app servers to spread requests across
Adds or changes headers on the request to the app
Forwards the request to the app behind nginx
Gives nginx the certificate to terminate TLS

remember: upstream lists the app servers, proxy_pass sends traffic to them, proxy_set_header shapes what they receive, and ssl_certificate lets nginx terminate TLS.

content.prompt: A load balancer terminates HTTPS and forwards plain HTTP to the app. After login the app redirects users to http://shop.hr/home. What should the app read to know the original request used HTTPS?

options.text: The X-Forwarded-Proto header set by the load balancer
The Host header of the incoming request
The port the app itself listens on

remember: Behind a TLS-terminating proxy the app sees plain HTTP; X-Forwarded-Proto from your own proxy tells it the original scheme.

content.statement: HTTP/3 runs over QUIC, which is built on UDP instead of TCP.

remember: HTTP/3 replaces TCP with QUIC over UDP, which handles reliability per stream and combines the transport and TLS handshakes.

content.prompt: What is the main improvement of HTTP/2 over HTTP/1.1?

options.text: Headers and bodies are sent as JSON instead of text
Many requests share one connection at the same time
It runs over UDP instead of TCP
Every request gets its own dedicated connection

remember: HTTP/2 multiplexes many requests over one connection as binary frames; HTTP/1.1 handles one response at a time per connection.

content.prompt: Match each HTTP version with how it uses connections.

right.text: Runs over QUIC, on UDP
Binary frames, many streams over one TCP connection
Opens a new TCP connection for each request by default
Keeps connections open; responses come back one at a time, in order

remember: 1.0 opened a connection per request, 1.1 reuses connections, 2 multiplexes streams over TCP, and 3 moves to QUIC over UDP.

content.prompt: Three of these were workarounds for HTTP/1.1's few parallel requests per host and lose most of their value with HTTP/2. Which one still matters just as much?

items.text: Domain sharding across img1. and img2. hosts
Combining icons into one sprite image
Inlining small images as data: URIs
Compressing responses with gzip or Brotli

remember: HTTP/2 makes extra requests cheap, so request-saving hacks like sharding and sprites lose their point, while fewer bytes still help.

content.prompt: Order what happens when a browser loads https://shop.hr over HTTP/2 for the first time.

steps.text: TLS handshake, where ALPN agrees on h2
DNS lookup of shop.hr
The GET is sent as a HEADERS frame on stream 1
TCP three-way handshake
The client sends the HTTP/2 connection preface and SETTINGS

remember: HTTP/2 is negotiated inside the TLS handshake through ALPN; after the connection preface every request is a stream of frames.
